how_a_silent_axis_was_decided: The client file's rule, applied unchanged and NOT restated here: a claim covers an axis only when an assertion's SUBJECT is the behaviour that axis names. What IS new on this leg is how often the rule bites on one axis of a two-axis check, and it bites the same way every time: eight of this file's red-OC edges are silent on an `http_status` axis and agree on a `jsonrpc_error_code` one. That is not a coincidence, it is the shape of this SDK's suite — `MCP.Server.DispatchTest` asserts below the transport and cannot see a status, and `MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTPStatelessTest` reads `error(conn)` rather than `conn.status` on every removed-method path. It is a real gap in our coverage and it is what puts those edges in 4b rather than leaving them able to reach 4a. C1c-ii's 16 edges bite a different way and it is worth recording because it changes what a `silent` MEANS on this file. Its two members make eight claims between them against multi-axis checks, and 29 of its 63 axis verdicts are `silent` — but almost none of those silences is a coverage gap. They are the arithmetic of A3 §1: a claim is ONE assertion, a check has up to five axes, and a member whose three claims cover three different axes of one check contributes three edges each silent on the other axes. Read edge by edge that looks like thin coverage; read member by member, `InputRequiredResultRequestStateIncomplete` has ALL FIVE of its axes covered by some claim of the stateless member. The file does not collapse them, because collapsing is what A3 §1 forbids — but a reader counting silences should count them per MEMBER, not per edge.
the_all_silent_case: THREE edges have EVERY axis silent. They are recorded and ESCALATED as `no_axis_contact`, never bucketed — A3 §2 rules that covering zero of one axis is no match rather than a partial one, generalised to N axes is exactly this, and A3 §3's table has no row for it. The client file has four of these and the rule is the same. What differs is that TWO of the three here are against a check that is RED at the accepted run (`ServerUnsupportedVersionError`), so the silence is not harmless: it is the precise reason our green tells us nothing about why the harness failed us. Each of the three says on its own record what the near-agreement was and where it stopped.
the_contradicting_edges:
SIX edges carry a `contradicts` verdict. FIVE are C1c-i's and are unchanged: the `initialize` pair (inherited from C1a) answering -32022 where the suite requires -32601; the `RequestMetaInvalid` pair answering -32022 where -32602 is required; and `subscriptions/listen` in JSON mode asserting HTTP 200 where the check's `http_status` axis requires 404 while AGREEING with the same check's `jsonrpc_error_code` axis. All five are 4a — red OC, green ET — and none escalates, because `(red, green, :contradicting)` is a row the ratified table has.

THE SIXTH IS C1c-ii's AND IT IS A DIFFERENT ANIMAL: it is the crosswalk's first contradiction against a GREEN check, and the first against `WireSchemaValid` on either leg. `MCP.Transport.StreamableHTTPStatelessTest/test tools/call input-required → retry with requestState → completion` asserts `is_list(first["inputRequests"])`, and the pinned schema's `InputRequests` is `type: object`. So our unit asserts, and passes on, a message that the check's own predicate would count as a violation — while the check is SUCCESS at the accepted run, because the harness ran against `conformance/server_handler.ex`, which sends a map and says in its own moduledoc that the SDK's `@spec` disagrees with the wire type. A contradiction against a GREEN check is NOT A BUCKET AT ALL, and that was measured rather than predicted: `MatchKey.bucket/3` sends `(:green, :green, :contradicting)` to `{:escalate, :inconsistent_verdict_pair}` (match_key.ex:554), so the edge leaves the bucket arithmetic entirely and lands in `escalations`. That is the right home for it — BOTH SIDES PASSED and they disagree, which is an inconsistency in the evidence rather than a verdict about the implementation — and it is the SERVER leg's first instance of that escalation (the client leg has three, all against `ClientMcpNameHeader_tools_call`). It is also why this finding is invisible to anyone reading bucket counts alone, and why it is written out here.
why_contradicts_and_not_silent: `how_a_silent_axis_was_decided` is conservative about claiming COVERAGE — a claim covers an axis only when an assertion's SUBJECT is the behaviour that axis names. It is NOT a rule for suppressing disagreement, and reading it that way would make it a rule for hiding exactly what a crosswalk exists to find. The client file states this and it is cited rather than restated; what is new here is that it now decides FIVE edges instead of three, and that on this leg the two readings give visibly different answers. Each of the five carries its own `why_contradicts_and_not_silent` where the judgement is not obvious from the evidence. C1c-ii's single contradiction is where the two readings come apart most sharply, and the edge carries its own `why_contradicts_and_not_silent` for it. The conservative reading would say the unit is `silent` on schema validity because it asserts a VALUE and not a VALIDATION. That reading is available and it is wrong: the axis quantifies over every message the implementation sent, the unit asserts the content of one such message, and the content it asserts is one the axis's predicate rejects. There is no grain at which the two are about different things — and the whole point of `how_a_silent_axis_was_decided` being about COVERAGE is that it must not become a way of not noticing this.
what_the_red_OC_population_did_and_did_n:
This is the first slice with a substantial red-OC population — 17 FAILURE and 13 SUCCESS among the declared checks, against 54 of 54 SUCCESS across the whole client leg — so it is the first at which buckets 4a and 4b are reachable on real data. Both are: 5 edges land 4a and 6 land 4b, out of 13 edges against a red check. A3 §3's THIRD combination, `(red, green, :full) -> :divergent_despite_agreement`, is STILL NOT LIVE, and that is a MEASUREMENT rather than an oversight. For it to fire, an edge would have to agree with EVERY axis of a red check. Every red check reached here either has a single axis our claims contradict (the RequestMetaInvalid family — we answer -32022 where -32602 is required) or has an `http_status` axis no unit of ours asserts: 8 of the 13 red-OC edges are silent on exactly that axis. The one unit that DOES assert a status asserts the wrong one, which is a contradiction and not an agreement. So the combination is unreachable from this slice's claims, and saying so is worth more than manufacturing an edge to reach it. The escalation is nonetheless EXERCISED on real server-stateless data by `conformance/controls/crosswalk_falsification_controls.exs escalations`, which takes a real 4b edge from this file, mutates its silent `http_status` axis to `agrees` in memory and requires the escalation to fire, then mutates the OC verdict to green on the same edge and requires it to STOP firing and bucket as 5. Both directions, because a rule that fires on everything is not discriminating and a control that only shows it firing cannot tell the difference.

C1c-ii ADDS NO RED-OC EDGE AT ALL, and the reason is a measurement rather than a choice. Of the 36 checks it declares, TWO are red at the accepted run and both are in one scenario: `InputRequiredResultNonToolIncomplete` (FAILURE) and that scenario's own `WireSchemaValid` (FAILURE). Both are about `prompts/get` returning an InputRequiredResult, and BOTH of this slice's members drive `tools/call` only — our SDK's `prompts/get` handler has no `{:input_required, …}` clause, which `conformance/server_handler.ex` records as a known limitation. So the family's red population is not merely unreached: there is no unit of ours that could reach it. A3 §3's `(red, green, :full)` — `divergent_despite_agreement` — is therefore STILL not live, and for a THIRD distinct reason: C1c-i's red checks were reached and contradicted, C1c-i's others had an `http_status` axis nobody asserts, and here the red checks are never exercised. the_empty_content_assertions_and_why_eve:
THREE OF THIS MODULE'S MEMBERS ASSERT THAT A tools/call RESULT'S CONTENT ARRAY IS EMPTY, and `ToolsCallSimpleText`'s `content_is_not_empty` axis requires it not to be. ALL THREE ARE SILENT AND NOT `contradicts`, and because `silent` is itself an assertion that can be the false one, the ground is written out here rather than left on three records. THE THREE WERE FOUND BY READING THE PREDICATE OVER THE WHOLE FILE RATHER THAN BY RECALLING WHICH FAMILIES HAVE IT: json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:294 (the C-2 not-injected member), json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:318 (the R-3 camelCase member) and json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:435 (the F-10 keyword-list member). The plan for this slice said `C-2's never-modified and the R-3 three`, which is four and is the wrong four; the measured set is these three.

THE ANTECEDENTS DIFFER, AND BOTH ARE VISIBLE IN THE SOURCE. The axis quantifies over the content array of a result returned by a tool that RETURNED CONTENT — the `tools-call-simple-text` scenario calls a fixture tool whose whole job is to produce a text block, and the axis asks whether the array it produced arrived non-empty. Each of the three units drives a handler it has just HANDED an empty content list, so the emptiness is forced by the unit's own construction and is not a behaviour of the SDK at all; what each unit is pinning is that the SDK did not ADD to the list — that an array-valued structuredContent, an unrecognised extras key or a dropped slot 3 leaves the handler's own content untouched. A server that injected a block would fail these units and SATISFY the axis. Two claims satisfied by opposite behaviours are not about the same case.

the_result_type_marker_the_suite_scores_:
THE SUITE SCORES `resultType` ON ONE PATH AND THE SDK PUTS IT ON EVERY RESULT — A COVERAGE ASYMMETRY THIS SLICE FOUND WHILE MEASURING SOMETHING ELSE. SEP-2322 makes `resultType` a member of the Result base rather than of InputRequiredResult: `lib/mcp/server/dispatch.ex:489-490` says so in terms and stamps the complete marker on every result this SDK returns. The official suite's only `resultType` scoring is `ResultTypeIncluded`, in the `input-required-result-result-type` scenario, and all four of its axes are taken over an INPUT-REQUIRED response: the scenario drives a call it expects to be answered input_required and reads the marker off that answer.

SO THE COMPLETE PATH IS SCORED BY NOTHING, and the two members that pin it here are an extras-map warning test (json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:340) and a dropped-slot-3 test (json_schema_2020_12_test.exs:436) — neither about MRTR, both asserting the marker incidentally while measuring a diagnostic. They agree with three of the check's four axes: the no-error and result-present axes, because the test's call helper returns the response's result member and an equality against a string cannot hold over an error or an absent result; and the PRESENCE axis, which is an IN test on the key and is satisfied whatever the value.

THE FOURTH AXIS IS SILENT AND THE JUDGEMENT IS THE SAME ONE THE EMPTY-CONTENT FAMILY RESTS ON. It requires the resultType of an INPUT-REQUIRED response to be the input_required marker; these results are completed calls carrying the complete marker, so the axis's antecedent does not hold of them. It is NOT the case that our SDK would fail that axis on the scenario's own call — C1c-ii's two edges on this same check agree with all four over a real input-required round trip — and if the axis is read as unconditional over every result the suite sees, these two edges are contradictions. The reading is stated so it can be contested; what is not in doubt is the coverage asymmetry underneath it.
